# dcb_layer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/dcb-layer/0.2.1/dcb_layer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#dcb)dcb

A [DCB-compliant](https://dcb.events) event store backed by [FoundationDB](https://www.foundationdb.org).

Events are appended atomically, assigned a globally ordered [ Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html) position,
and indexed for fast retrieval by type, tags, or both.
Optimistic concurrency is enforced through

[s that fail the write if matching events appeared since the caller last read.](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html)

`AppendCondition`[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use dcb_layer::{Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // 1. Open a FoundationDB database (see foundationdb-rs for setup).
    let _network = unsafe { foundationdb::boot() };
    let db = foundationdb::Database::default().unwrap();
    // 2. Create a namespaced store — namespace isolates data within one FDB cluster.
    let store = FdbStore::new(db, "my-app");
    // 3. Append events (no condition = unconditional write).
    let event = Event::new(
        "OrderPlaced",
        ["order:42", "customer:7"],
        b"{\"total\":99}".as_slice(),
    );
    let position = store.append(vec![event], vec![]).await.unwrap();
    // 4. Read events back — filter by type, tags, or both.
    let results = store
        .read(
            Query {
                items: vec![QueryItem {
                    types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
                    tags: vec!["customer:7".into()],
                }],
            },
            None,
        )
        .await
        .unwrap();
    println!("Found {} event(s), first at {:?}", results.len(), results[0].position);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core concepts

[§](https://docs.rs#event)Event

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) carries three fields, constructed via

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html#method.new)

`Event::new`| Field | Accepts | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `type_name` | `&str`/`String` | Required, non-empty (e.g. `"OrderPlaced"`) |
| `tags` | any iterable of strings | Up to 10 tags; `"_"`is reserved |
| `data` | `&[u8]`/`Vec<u8>` | Opaque bytes — encode however you like |

Tags are free-form strings. A common convention is `"entity:id"` (e.g. `"order:42"`),
but the store treats them as opaque labels.

[§](https://docs.rs#query)Query

A [ Query](https://docs.rs/struct.Query.html) is a list of

[s joined by](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryItem.html)

`QueryItem`**OR**. Each item matches events that satisfy

**all**of its constraints:

- `types`— event’s- `type_name`must be one of these (empty = any type)
- `tags`— event must carry- **all**of these tags (empty = any tags)

Every item must specify at least one type or one tag.

```
use dcb_layer::{Query, QueryItem};
// Match OrderPlaced OR OrderCancelled events tagged with order:42
let query = Query {
    items: vec![
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
        QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderCancelled".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] },
    ],
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#appendcondition)AppendCondition

An [ AppendCondition](https://docs.rs/struct.AppendCondition.html) guards a write with an optimistic-concurrency check:
the

`append` call fails with [if any event matching](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html#variant.AppendConditionFailed)

`Error::AppendConditionFailed``query` exists **after**the

`after` position (or at all, when `after` is `None`).The typical pattern:

- Read events matching your query → note the last position seen.
- Build your decision model from those events.
- Append new events with `after = last_position`to guard against concurrent writes.

```
use dcb_layer::{AppendCondition, Event, FdbStore, Query, QueryItem};
// 1. Read events and note the last position seen.
let results = store.read(
    Query { items: vec![QueryItem { types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()], tags: vec!["order:42".into()] }] },
    None,
).await.unwrap();
let last_position = results.last().map(|e| e.position);
// 2. Append new events — fail if a concurrent write snuck in after last_position.
let condition = AppendCondition {
    query: Query {
        items: vec![QueryItem {
            types: vec!["OrderPlaced".into()],
            tags: vec!["order:42".into()],
        }],
    },
    after: last_position,
};
store.append(vec![Event::new("OrderPlaced", ["order:42"], b"".as_slice())], vec![condition]).await.unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#readoptions)ReadOptions

[ ReadOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.ReadOptions.html) controls pagination and ordering:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | `0`(unlimited) | Maximum events to return |
| `after` | `None` | Only return events after this position |
| `reverse` | `false` | Newest-first when `true` |

[§](https://docs.rs#limits)Limits

| Constraint | Value |
|---|---|
| Max events per `append`call | 65 535 |
| Max tags per event | 10 |
| Reserved tag value | `"_"` |

[§](https://docs.rs#practical-sizing)Practical sizing

Each event writes one index key per **subset** of its tags (2^n keys for
n tags — up to 1 024 for 10 tags). All writes of an `append` call share one
FDB transaction, which is capped at 10 MB of affected data and 5 seconds —
keep batches small when events carry many tags.

Reads run in a single FDB transaction too: an unbounded [ FdbStore::read](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read)
or

[over a large store fails with](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.read_all)

`FdbStore::read_all``transaction_too_old` (FDB error 1007) after a bounded number of retries.
Paginate with

`ReadOptions``limit` + `after`.Subscription cursors ([ FdbStore::set_cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.FdbStore.html#method.set_cursor)) are last-writer-wins; run
one consumer per cursor name or coordinate externally.

[§](https://docs.rs#foundationdb-setup)FoundationDB setup

This crate wraps the [ foundationdb](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) crate.
You are responsible for:

- installing and running an FDB cluster
- calling `unsafe { foundationdb::boot() }`once at startup (keeps the network thread alive)
- opening a `foundationdb::Database``FdbStore::new`

Refer to the [foundationdb-rs documentation](https://docs.rs/foundationdb) and
the [FoundationDB developer guide](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/getting-started-linux.html)
for cluster setup and client configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#fdb-api-version)FDB API version

The default Cargo feature targets FDB 7.4. To use FDB 7.3, disable the default features:

`dcb-layer = { version = "...", default-features = false, features = ["fdb-7_3"] }`The feature selects the C API headers compiled against; a newer `libfdb_c` is backward compatible.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Versionstamp](https://docs.rs/type.Versionstamp.html)
- 12-byte globally unique, monotonically increasing position. Bytes 0–9: FDB transaction version (big-endian). Bytes 10–11: user version = batch index (big-endian u16).

# hdf5_metno - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hdf5-metno/0.13.0/hdf5_metno/

## Expand description

HDF5 for Rust.

This crate provides thread-safe Rust bindings and high-level wrappers for the `HDF5`
library API. Some of the features include:

- Thread-safety with non-threadsafe libhdf5 builds guaranteed via reentrant mutexes.
- Native representation of most HDF5 types, including variable-length strings and arrays.
- Derive-macro for automatic mapping of user structs and enums to `HDF5`types.
- Multi-dimensional array reading/writing interface via `ndarray`.

Direct low-level bindings are also available and provided in the `hdf5-sys` crate.

Requires `HDF5` library of version 1.8.4 or later. Newer versions will enable additional
features of the library. Such items are marked in the documentation with a version number
indicating the required version of `HDF5`. The `have-direct` and `have-parallel` features
also indicates `HDF5` functionality.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [dataset](https://docs.rs/dataset/index.html)
- Multi-dimensional datasets.
- [datatype](https://docs.rs/datatype/index.html)
- Datatype objects for defining the layout of a data element.
- [file](https://docs.rs/file/index.html)
- HDF5 file objects.
- [filters](https://docs.rs/filters/index.html)
- Filters for data compression and validation during file I/O.
- [plist](https://docs.rs/plist/index.html)

# swarm_abm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/swarm-abm/0.3.0/swarm_abm/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#swarm-abm)swarm-abm

Spatial agent-based modeling (ABM) engine: agents on a 2D grid, configurable scheduling, time-series data collection, and deterministic reproducibility (same seed → same results).

[§](https://docs.rs#concepts)Concepts

- `Agent`
- `Model`
- `Grid2D`
- `Schedule`- `decide`with an immutable model +- `apply`).
- `DataCollector`
- `Simulation`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-random-walkers)Example: random walkers

```
use swarm_abm::prelude::*;
struct Walker {
    pos: Pos,
}
struct World {
    agents: AgentSet<Walker>,
    visits: Grid2D<u32>,
}
impl Agent for Walker {
    type Model = World;
    fn step(&mut self, _id: AgentId, world: &mut World, rng: &mut SimRng) {
        if let Some(dest) =
            world.visits.random_neighbor(self.pos, Neighborhood::Moore, rng)
        {
            self.pos = dest;
            world.visits[self.pos] += 1;
        }
    }
}
impl Model for World {
    type Agent = Walker;
    fn agents(&self) -> &AgentSet<Walker> {
        &self.agents
    }
    fn agents_mut(&mut self) -> &mut AgentSet<Walker> {
        &mut self.agents
    }
}
let mut agents = AgentSet::new();
agents.insert(Walker { pos: Pos::new(5, 5) });
let visits = Grid2D::new(10, 10).with_torus(true);
let mut sim = Simulation::new(World { agents, visits }, 42);
sim.add_reporter("total_visits", |w: &World| {
    w.visits.iter().map(|(_, &v)| f64::from(v)).sum()
});
sim.run(100);
assert_eq!(sim.step_count(), 100);
assert_eq!(sim.data().series("total_visits").unwrap().last(), Some(&100.0));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [agent](https://docs.rs/agent/index.html)
- `Agent`- `AgentSet`
- [batch](https://docs.rs/batch/index.html)
- Running **ensembles**and**parameter sweeps**.
- [continuous](https://docs.rs/continuous/index.html)
- **Continuous**2D space for off-lattice ABMs: movement,- *flocking*, particles — where position is real-valued (- `f64`), not a cell.
- [data](https://docs.rs/data/index.html)
- Per-step (`DataCollector``AgentDataCollector`
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)
- **Network**(graph) space for network ABMs: contagion on social networks, propagation in infrastructure, information diffusion, mobility.
- [grid](https://docs.rs/grid/index.html)
- Dense 2D grid with Moore and Von Neumann neighborhoods.
- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- `Model`
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the types needed to define and run a model.
- [rng](https://docs.rs/rng/index.html)
- Seedable, deterministic random number generation.
- [schedule](https://docs.rs/schedule/index.html)
- Activation order of agents at each step.
- [sim](https://docs.rs/sim/index.html)
- Runner for the simulation: `Simulation`

# capsudod-pwauth 0.1.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/capsudod-pwauth/0.1.2

# capsudo-rs

`sudo`, but [object-capability style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-capability_model) — a Rust reimplementation of
[capsudo](https://github.com/kaniini/capsudo) built so the capability channel
can be **proxied across  Edera Protect zones over IDM**, not just a
local Unix socket.

## The idea

Privilege is not granted by a setuid bit. A privileged daemon (`capsudod`) is
started ahead of time, already holding the privilege you want to delegate, and
bound to a *transport endpoint*. Whoever can reach that endpoint can invoke the
capability. The endpoint **is** the capability.

In the original, the endpoint is always an `AF_UNIX` socket whose file
permissions decide who may connect. Here the transport is abstracted: the same
protocol and the same client/daemon logic run unchanged over a local Unix
socket *or* a cross-zone IDM channel, so a capability held in one Edera zone can
be exposed to another without either side knowing the difference.

## What this enables

The motivating deployment is autonomous AI agents. An agent is sandboxed precisely because what it runs cannot be fully trusted, yet real work needs a few privileged operations: push this image, run that deploy script, restart a wedged service. The conventional escapes all grant ambient, stealable authority. A kubeconfig or SSH key mounted into the sandbox works from anywhere once exfiltrated, and sudo inside the sandbox puts privilege in the one place most likely to be prompt-injected.

capsudo restates the problem in object-capability terms. The agent's zone
holds no credentials at all; it holds an endpoint, and reaching the endpoint
is the permission. The daemon side fixes the command and environment (`-f`,
`-E`), so even a fully compromised client can only cause the pre-approved
operation to run. There is nothing to steal: the endpoint does not exist
outside the zone it was granted to, and its effect cannot be broadened from
the client side.

For the caller nothing changes: prefix a command, keep ordinary
stdin/stdout/stderr, exit codes, and fully interactive ptys, whether the
daemon is local or in another zone. In an Edera Protect deployment the grants
are declarative: the zone agent launches and manages the attenuated `capsudod`
instances from configuration and proxies an endpoint like `/run/cap/<name>`
into each authorized zone over IDM.

## Why a rewrite was needed for cross-zone

Two things in the original assume a shared kernel:

-
**Descriptor passing.**The caller's stdin/stdout/stderr are handed to the daemon over`SCM_RIGHTS`. File descriptors are meaningless across a zone boundary. Here the transport layer papers over that — real`SCM_RIGHTS`locally,**simulated**descriptor passing (stream multiplexing + local pipe ends) cross-zone — transparently, so client and daemon never learn which happened.
-
**The interactive pty.**The original allocates the pty on the*client*and ships the slave. A pty slave is a real terminal; a socket pair (all a cross-zone link can fabricate) is not. So the pty is allocated on the**daemon**side instead: the child always gets a genuine controlling terminal in its own zone, and only a byte stream plus window-size updates cross the channel. (The C version was updated to match.)

## Workspace layout

| Crate | Role |
|---|---|
| `capsudo-proto` | Transport-agnostic wire protocol: message types, portable fixed-endianness framing. No I/O. |
| `capsudo-transport` | `Transport`/`Listener`traits + implementations:`unix`(real`SCM_RIGHTS`),`mux`(simulated fd-passing over any byte channel),`fakeidm`(throwaway TCP cross-zone stub, feature`fakeidm`). |
| `capsudo-core` | Client and daemon session logic, written entirely against the traits. |
| `capsudo` | Client binary. |
| `capsudod` | Daemon binary (listening, or one-shot on stdin). |
| `capsudod-pwauth` | Authenticating front-end: shadow-password check, then chain to `capsudod`. Local sockets only: it identifies the caller via`SO_PEERCRED`, which does not exist across zones. |

## Build & test

```
cargo build
cargo test
cargo build --features capsudo-transport/fakeidm    # include the fake IDM stub
```
## Command-line

```
# Delegate "run anything" to whoever can reach the socket:
capsudod -S /run/capsudo/sudo -o root:wheel -m 0770 &
capsudo  -S /run/capsudo/sudo -- id
# Pin an exact command (client args ignored):
capsudod -S /run/capsudo/reboot -f /sbin/reboot &
capsudo  -S /run/capsudo/reboot
# Require a password first, then chain to capsudod:
capsudod-pwauth -S /run/capsudo/auth -o root:wheel -m 0770 -- capsudod &
capsudo -S /run/capsudo/auth -- id
```
See `CLAUDE.md` for the architecture in depth.

---

# capsudo_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capsudo-core/0.1.2/capsudo_core/

## Expand description

Client and daemon session logic for capsudo, generic over any
[ Transport](https://docs.rs/capsudo-transport/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capsudo_transport/traits/trait.Transport.html).

This crate contains the actual capsudo behaviour — the configuration handshake, attenuation policy, and program execution — with no knowledge of whether it is talking over a local Unix socket or a cross-zone IDM channel.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientRequest.html)- Request
- What the client is asking the daemon to do.
- [Daemon](https://docs.rs/struct.DaemonConfig.html)- Config
- Daemon-side policy applied to every session.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Core](https://docs.rs/enum.CoreError.html)- Error
- Errors arising from the client or daemon session logic.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/enum.SessionOutcome.html)- Outcome
- How a client session ended.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_winsize.html)- winsize
- Reads the current terminal dimensions from `fd`.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_client.html)- client
- Runs a client session to completion and returns the target program’s exit
status. Treats an authentication challenge as an error; use `run_session`
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_session.html)- session
- Runs one client session, optionally presenting `secret`for authentication.
- [serve_](https://docs.rs/fn.serve_connection.html)- connection
- Serves a single client connection: receives configuration, runs the program, and reports the exit status.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Convenience result alias for core operations.

# capsudo_transport - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/capsudo-transport/0.1.2/capsudo_transport/

## Expand description

Transport abstraction for capsudo.

The capsudo protocol ([ capsudo_proto](https://docs.rs/capsudo-proto/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/capsudo_proto/index.html)) is spoken over

*some*channel. This crate defines the

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html)

`Transport`[traits that abstract that channel, plus concrete implementations.](https://docs.rs/trait.Listener.html)

`Listener``capsudo` and `capsudod` are written
against the traits alone, so the same logic runs over:- `unix`- `AF_UNIX`socket, using real- `SCM_RIGHTS`to delegate the caller’s stdio descriptors; and
- a cross-zone Edera Protect IDM channel (built into Protect itself), which
*simulates*descriptor passing by multiplexing stream data — transparently, so neither client nor daemon needs to know. [`fakeidm`] is a throwaway TCP-backed stand-in for exercising that path on one host.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use unix::`- [UnixListener](https://docs.rs/unix/struct.UnixListener.html);
- `pub use unix::`- [UnixTransport](https://docs.rs/unix/struct.UnixTransport.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [mux](https://docs.rs/mux/index.html)
- A multiplexing transport that *simulates*`SCM_RIGHTS`over any plain byte channel.
- [ownerspec](https://docs.rs/ownerspec/index.html)
- Parsing of `user[:group]`ownership specs and octal permission modes for listener sockets — the access-control knobs (`-o`/`-m`) shared by the daemons.
- [unix](https://docs.rs/unix/index.html)
- Local transport over an `AF_UNIX``SOCK_STREAM`socket.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FdSpec](https://docs.rs/struct.FdSpec.html)
- A descriptor offered to `Transport::send`
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/struct.PeerCred.html)- Cred
- Peer credentials, where the transport can establish them.
- [Received](https://docs.rs/struct.Received.html)
- A message received from a transport, together with any file descriptors that accompanied it.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [FdDir](https://docs.rs/enum.FdDir.html)
- Which way bytes flow through a delegated descriptor, from the perspective of the side that currently holds it.
- [Transport](https://docs.rs/enum.TransportError.html)- Error
- Errors produced by a `Transport``Listener`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Control](https://docs.rs/trait.ControlSender.html)- Sender
- A detached sink for fd-less control messages, usable from another task while
the owning `Transport``recv`
- [Listener](https://docs.rs/trait.Listener.html)
- Accepts inbound capsudo connections, yielding a `Transport`
- [Transport](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html)
- A bidirectional, message-oriented capsudo channel that can also convey file descriptors out-of-band.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Convenience result alias for transport operations.

# stablebond_events - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stablebond-events/3.0.7/stablebond_events/

An Anchor generated module, providing a set of structs
mirroring the structs deriving Accounts, where each field is
a Pubkey. This is useful for specifying accounts for a client.

An Anchor generated module containing the program’s set of
instructions, where each method handler in the #[program] mod is
associated with a struct defining the input arguments to the
method. These should be used directly, when one wants to serialize
Anchor instruction data, for example, when speciying
instructions on a client.

The Anchor codegen exposes a programming model where a user defines
a set of methods inside of a #[program] module in a way similar
to writing RPC request handlers. The macro then generates a bunch of
code wrapping these user defined methods into something that can be
executed on Solana.

# rkyv 0.8.17 - Docs.rs

#
                    rkyv 0.8.17

                Zero-copy deserialization framework for Rust

---

# rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rkyv/0.8.17/target-redirect/rkyv/

## Expand description

rkyv is a zero-copy deserialization framework for Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

rkyv uses Rust’s powerful trait system to serialize data without reflection. Many zero-copy deserialization frameworks use external schemas and heavily restrict the available data types. By contrast, rkyv allows all serialized types to be defined in code and can serialize a wide variety of types that other frameworks cannot.

rkyv scales to highly-capable as well as highly-restricted environments. Not only does rkyv support “no-std” builds for targets without a standard library implementation, it also supports “no-alloc” builds for targets where allocations cannot be made.

rkyv supports limited in-place data mutation, and so can access and update data without ever deserializing back to native types. When rkyv’s in-place mutation is too limited, rkyv also provides ergonomic and performant deserialization back into native types.

rkyv prioritizes performance, and is one of the fastest serialization frameworks available. All of rkyv’s features can be individually enabled and disabled, so you only pay for what you use. Additionally, all of rkyv’s zero-copy types are designed to have little to no overhead. In most cases, rkyv’s types will have exactly the same performance as native types.

See the [rkyv book](https://rkyv.org) for guide-level documentation.
See [the examples directory](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv/tree/main/rkyv/examples) for usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#components)Components

rkyv has [a hash map implementation](https://docs.rs/collections/swiss_table/map/struct.ArchivedHashMap.html) that is built for zero-copy
deserialization, with the same lookup and iteration performance as the
standard library hash maps. The hash map implementation is based on
[Swiss Tables](https://abseil.io/about/design/swisstables) and uses a target-independent version of FxHash to ensure
that all targets compute the same hashes.

It also has [a B-tree implementation](https://docs.rs/collections/btree_map/struct.ArchivedBTreeMap.html) that has the same performance
characteristics as the standard library B-tree maps. Its compact
representation and localized data storage is best-suited for very large
amounts of data.

rkyv supports [shared pointers](https://docs.rs/rc/index.html) by default, and is able to serialize and
deserialize them without duplicating the underlying data. Shared pointers
which point to the same data when serialized will still point to the same
data when deserialized. By default, rkyv only supports non-cyclic data
structures.

Alongside its [unchecked API](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked.html), rkyv also provides optional [validation](https://docs.rs/fn.access.html) so
you can ensure safety and data integrity at the cost of some overhead.
Because checking serialized data can generally be done without allocations,
the cost of checking and zero-copy access can be much lower than that of
traditional deserialization.

rkyv is trait-oriented from top to bottom, and is made to be extended with custom and specialized types. Serialization, deserialization, and validation traits all accept generic context types, making it easy to add new capabilities without degrading ergonomics.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

rkyv has several feature flags which can be used to modify its behavior. By
default, rkyv enables the `std`, `alloc`, and `bytecheck` features.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-control)Format control

These features control how rkyv formats its serialized data. Enabling and disabling these features may change rkyv’s serialized format, and as such can cause previously-serialized data to become unreadable. Enabling format control features that are not the default should be considered a breaking change to rkyv’s serialized format.

Binaries should consider explicitly choosing format control options from the start, even though doing so is not required. This ensures that developers stay informed about the specific choices being made, and prevents any unexpected compatibility issues with libraries they depend on.

Libraries should avoid enabling format control features unless they intend to only support rkyv when those specific format control features are enabled. In general, libraries should be able to support all format control options if they use rkyv’s exported types and aliases.

[§](https://docs.rs#endianness)Endianness

If an endianness feature is not enabled, rkyv will use little-endian byte ordering by default.

- `little_endian`: Forces data serialization to use little-endian byte ordering. This optimizes serialized data for little-endian architectures.
- `big_endian`: Forces data serialization to use big-endian byte ordering. This optimizes serialized data for big-endian architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#alignment)Alignment

If an alignment feature is not enabled, rkyv will use aligned primitives by default.

- `aligned`: Forces data serialization to use aligned primitives. This adds alignment requirements for accessing data and prevents rkyv from working with unaligned data.
- `unaligned`: Forces data serialization to use unaligned primitives. This removes alignment requirements for accessing data and allows rkyv to work with unaligned data more easily.

[§](https://docs.rs#pointer-width)Pointer width

If a pointer width feature is not enabled, rkyv will serialize `isize` and
`usize` as 32-bit integers by default.

- `pointer_width_16`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 16-bit integers. This is intended to be used only for small data sizes and may not handle large amounts of data.
- `pointer_width_32`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 32-bit integers. This is a good choice for most data, and balances the storage overhead with support for large data sizes.
- `pointer_width_64`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 64-bit integers. This is intended to be used only for extremely large data sizes and may cause unnecessary data bloat for smaller amounts of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#functionality)Functionality

These features enable more built-in functionality and provide more powerful and ergonomic APIs. Enabling and disabling these features does not change rkyv’s serialized format.

- `alloc`: Enables support for the- `alloc`crate. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables standard library support. Enabled by default.
- `bytecheck`: Enables data validation through- `bytecheck`. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

rkyv provides integrations for some common crates by default. In the future, crates should depend on rkyv and provide their own integration. Enabling and disabling these features does not change rkyv’s serialized format.

- `arrayvec-0_7`
- `bytes-1`
- `hashbrown-0_14`
- `hashbrown-0_15`
- `hashbrown-0_16`
- `hashbrown-0_17`
- `indexmap-2`
- `smallvec-1`
- `smol_str-0_2`
- `smol_str-0_3`
- `thin-vec-0_2`
- `tinyvec-1`
- `triomphe-0_1`
- `uuid-1`

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

Serialized data can be accessed later as long as:

- The underlying schema has not changed
- The serialized format has not been changed by format control features
- The data was serialized by a semver-compatible version of rkyv

# rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/index.html

## Expand description

rkyv is a zero-copy deserialization framework for Rust.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

rkyv uses Rust’s powerful trait system to serialize data without reflection. Many zero-copy deserialization frameworks use external schemas and heavily restrict the available data types. By contrast, rkyv allows all serialized types to be defined in code and can serialize a wide variety of types that other frameworks cannot.

rkyv scales to highly-capable as well as highly-restricted environments. Not only does rkyv support “no-std” builds for targets without a standard library implementation, it also supports “no-alloc” builds for targets where allocations cannot be made.

rkyv supports limited in-place data mutation, and so can access and update data without ever deserializing back to native types. When rkyv’s in-place mutation is too limited, rkyv also provides ergonomic and performant deserialization back into native types.

rkyv prioritizes performance, and is one of the fastest serialization frameworks available. All of rkyv’s features can be individually enabled and disabled, so you only pay for what you use. Additionally, all of rkyv’s zero-copy types are designed to have little to no overhead. In most cases, rkyv’s types will have exactly the same performance as native types.

See the [rkyv book](https://rkyv.org) for guide-level documentation.
See [the examples directory](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv/tree/main/rkyv/examples) for usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#components)Components

rkyv has [a hash map implementation](https://docs.rs/collections/swiss_table/map/struct.ArchivedHashMap.html) that is built for zero-copy
deserialization, with the same lookup and iteration performance as the
standard library hash maps. The hash map implementation is based on
[Swiss Tables](https://abseil.io/about/design/swisstables) and uses a target-independent version of FxHash to ensure
that all targets compute the same hashes.

It also has [a B-tree implementation](https://docs.rs/collections/btree_map/struct.ArchivedBTreeMap.html) that has the same performance
characteristics as the standard library B-tree maps. Its compact
representation and localized data storage is best-suited for very large
amounts of data.

rkyv supports [shared pointers](https://docs.rs/rc/index.html) by default, and is able to serialize and
deserialize them without duplicating the underlying data. Shared pointers
which point to the same data when serialized will still point to the same
data when deserialized. By default, rkyv only supports non-cyclic data
structures.

Alongside its [unchecked API](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked.html), rkyv also provides optional [validation](https://docs.rs/fn.access.html) so
you can ensure safety and data integrity at the cost of some overhead.
Because checking serialized data can generally be done without allocations,
the cost of checking and zero-copy access can be much lower than that of
traditional deserialization.

rkyv is trait-oriented from top to bottom, and is made to be extended with custom and specialized types. Serialization, deserialization, and validation traits all accept generic context types, making it easy to add new capabilities without degrading ergonomics.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

rkyv has several feature flags which can be used to modify its behavior. By
default, rkyv enables the `std`, `alloc`, and `bytecheck` features.

[§](https://docs.rs#format-control)Format control

These features control how rkyv formats its serialized data. Enabling and disabling these features may change rkyv’s serialized format, and as such can cause previously-serialized data to become unreadable. Enabling format control features that are not the default should be considered a breaking change to rkyv’s serialized format.

Binaries should consider explicitly choosing format control options from the start, even though doing so is not required. This ensures that developers stay informed about the specific choices being made, and prevents any unexpected compatibility issues with libraries they depend on.

Libraries should avoid enabling format control features unless they intend to only support rkyv when those specific format control features are enabled. In general, libraries should be able to support all format control options if they use rkyv’s exported types and aliases.

[§](https://docs.rs#endianness)Endianness

If an endianness feature is not enabled, rkyv will use little-endian byte ordering by default.

- `little_endian`: Forces data serialization to use little-endian byte ordering. This optimizes serialized data for little-endian architectures.
- `big_endian`: Forces data serialization to use big-endian byte ordering. This optimizes serialized data for big-endian architectures.

[§](https://docs.rs#alignment)Alignment

If an alignment feature is not enabled, rkyv will use aligned primitives by default.

- `aligned`: Forces data serialization to use aligned primitives. This adds alignment requirements for accessing data and prevents rkyv from working with unaligned data.
- `unaligned`: Forces data serialization to use unaligned primitives. This removes alignment requirements for accessing data and allows rkyv to work with unaligned data more easily.

[§](https://docs.rs#pointer-width)Pointer width

If a pointer width feature is not enabled, rkyv will serialize `isize` and
`usize` as 32-bit integers by default.

- `pointer_width_16`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 16-bit integers. This is intended to be used only for small data sizes and may not handle large amounts of data.
- `pointer_width_32`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 32-bit integers. This is a good choice for most data, and balances the storage overhead with support for large data sizes.
- `pointer_width_64`: Serializes- `isize`and- `usize`as 64-bit integers. This is intended to be used only for extremely large data sizes and may cause unnecessary data bloat for smaller amounts of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#functionality)Functionality

These features enable more built-in functionality and provide more powerful and ergonomic APIs. Enabling and disabling these features does not change rkyv’s serialized format.

- `alloc`: Enables support for the- `alloc`crate. Enabled by default.
- `std`: Enables standard library support. Enabled by default.
- `bytecheck`: Enables data validation through- `bytecheck`. Enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

rkyv provides integrations for some common crates by default. In the future, crates should depend on rkyv and provide their own integration. Enabling and disabling these features does not change rkyv’s serialized format.

- `arrayvec-0_7`
- `bytes-1`
- `hashbrown-0_14`
- `hashbrown-0_15`
- `hashbrown-0_16`
- `hashbrown-0_17`
- `indexmap-2`
- `smallvec-1`
- `smol_str-0_2`
- `smol_str-0_3`
- `thin-vec-0_2`
- `tinyvec-1`
- `triomphe-0_1`
- `uuid-1`

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

Serialized data can be accessed later as long as:

- The underlying schema has not changed
- The serialized format has not been changed by format control features
- The data was serialized by a semver-compatible version of rkyv

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/src/rkyv/lib.rs.html

# rkyv/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! rkyv is a zero-copy deserialization framework for Rust.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! ## Overview
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! rkyv uses Rust's powerful trait system to serialize data without reflection.
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Many zero-copy deserialization frameworks use external schemas and heavily
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! restrict the available data types. By contrast, rkyv allows all serialized
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! types to be defined in code and can serialize a wide variety of types that
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! other frameworks cannot.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! rkyv scales to highly-capable as well as highly-restricted environments. Not
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! only does rkyv support "no-std" builds for targets without a standard
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! library implementation, it also supports "no-alloc" builds for targets where
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! allocations cannot be made.
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! rkyv supports limited in-place data mutation, and so can access and update
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! data without ever deserializing back to native types. When rkyv's in-place
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! mutation is too limited, rkyv also provides ergonomic and performant
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! deserialization back into native types.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! rkyv prioritizes performance, and is one of the fastest serialization
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! frameworks available. All of rkyv's features can be individually enabled and
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! disabled, so you only pay for what you use. Additionally, all of rkyv's
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! zero-copy types are designed to have little to no overhead. In most cases,
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! rkyv's types will have exactly the same performance as native types.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! See the [rkyv book] for guide-level documentation.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! See [the examples directory][1] for usage examples.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! [rkyv book]: https://rkyv.org
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! [1]: https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv/tree/main/rkyv/examples
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! ## Components
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! rkyv has [a hash map implementation] that is built for zero-copy
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! deserialization, with the same lookup and iteration performance as the
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! standard library hash maps. The hash map implementation is based on
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! [Swiss Tables] and uses a target-independent version of FxHash to ensure
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! that all targets compute the same hashes.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! It also has [a B-tree implementation] that has the same performance
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! characteristics as the standard library B-tree maps. Its compact
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! representation and localized data storage is best-suited for very large
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! amounts of data.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! rkyv supports [shared pointers] by default, and is able to serialize and
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! deserialize them without duplicating the underlying data. Shared pointers
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! which point to the same data when serialized will still point to the same
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! data when deserialized. By default, rkyv only supports non-cyclic data
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! structures.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! Alongside its [unchecked API], rkyv also provides optional [validation] so
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! you can ensure safety and data integrity at the cost of some overhead.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! Because checking serialized data can generally be done without allocations,
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! the cost of checking and zero-copy access can be much lower than that of
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! traditional deserialization.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! rkyv is trait-oriented from top to bottom, and is made to be extended with
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! custom and specialized types. Serialization, deserialization, and
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! validation traits all accept generic context types, making it easy to add
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! new capabilities without degrading ergonomics.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! [a hash map implementation]: collections::swiss_table::ArchivedHashMap
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! [Swiss Tables]: https://abseil.io/about/design/swisstables
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! [a B-tree implementation]: collections::btree_map::ArchivedBTreeMap
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! [shared pointers]: rc
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! [unchecked API]: access_unchecked
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! [validation]: access
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! ## Features
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! rkyv has several feature flags which can be used to modify its behavior. By
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! default, rkyv enables the `std`, `alloc`, and `bytecheck` features.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! ### Format control
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! These features control how rkyv formats its serialized data. Enabling and
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! disabling these features may change rkyv's serialized format, and as such
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! can cause previously-serialized data to become unreadable. Enabling format
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! control features that are not the default should be considered a breaking
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! change to rkyv's serialized format.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! Binaries should consider explicitly choosing format control options from the
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! start, even though doing so is not required. This ensures that developers
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! stay informed about the specific choices being made, and prevents any
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! unexpected compatibility issues with libraries they depend on.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! Libraries should avoid enabling format control features unless they intend
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! to only support rkyv when those specific format control features are
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! enabled. In general, libraries should be able to support all format control
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! options if they use rkyv's exported types and aliases.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! #### Endianness
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! If an endianness feature is not enabled, rkyv will use little-endian byte
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! ordering by default.
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! - `little_endian`: Forces data serialization to use little-endian byte
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!   ordering. This optimizes serialized data for little-endian architectures.
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! - `big_endian`: Forces data serialization to use big-endian byte ordering.
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!   This optimizes serialized data for big-endian architectures.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! #### Alignment
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! If an alignment feature is not enabled, rkyv will use aligned primitives by
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! default.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! - `aligned`: Forces data serialization to use aligned primitives. This adds
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!   alignment requirements for accessing data and prevents rkyv from working
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!   with unaligned data.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! - `unaligned`: Forces data serialization to use unaligned primitives. This
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!   removes alignment requirements for accessing data and allows rkyv to work
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!   with unaligned data more easily.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! #### Pointer width
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! If a pointer width feature is not enabled, rkyv will serialize `isize` and
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! `usize` as 32-bit integers by default.
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! - `pointer_width_16`: Serializes `isize` and `usize` as 16-bit integers.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!   This is intended to be used only for small data sizes and may not handle
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!   large amounts of data.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! - `pointer_width_32`: Serializes `isize` and `usize` as 32-bit integers.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!   This is a good choice for most data, and balances the storage overhead
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!   with support for large data sizes.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! - `pointer_width_64`: Serializes `isize` and `usize` as 64-bit integers.
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!   This is intended to be used only for extremely large data sizes and may
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!   cause unnecessary data bloat for smaller amounts of data.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! ### Functionality
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! These features enable more built-in functionality and provide more powerful
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! and ergonomic APIs. Enabling and disabling these features does not change
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! rkyv's serialized format.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! - `alloc`: Enables support for the `alloc` crate. Enabled by default.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! - `std`: Enables standard library support. Enabled by default.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! - `bytecheck`: Enables data validation through `bytecheck`. Enabled by
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!   default.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ### Crates
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! rkyv provides integrations for some common crates by default. In the future,
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! crates should depend on rkyv and provide their own integration. Enabling and
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! disabling these features does not change rkyv's serialized format.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! - [`arrayvec-0_7`](https://docs.rs/arrayvec/0.7)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! - [`bytes-1`](https://docs.rs/bytes/1)
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! - [`hashbrown-0_14`](https://docs.rs/hashbrown/0.14)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! - [`hashbrown-0_15`](https://docs.rs/hashbrown/0.15)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! - [`hashbrown-0_16`](https://docs.rs/hashbrown/0.16)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! - [`hashbrown-0_17`](https://docs.rs/hashbrown/0.17)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! - [`indexmap-2`](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2)
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! - [`smallvec-1`](https://docs.rs/smallvec/1)
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! - [`smol_str-0_2`](https://docs.rs/smol_str/0.2)
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! - [`smol_str-0_3`](https://docs.rs/smol_str/0.3)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! - [`thin-vec-0_2`](https://docs.rs/thin-vec/0.2)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! - [`tinyvec-1`](https://docs.rs/tinyvec/1)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! - [`triomphe-0_1`](https://docs.rs/triomphe/0.1)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! - [`uuid-1`](https://docs.rs/uuid/1)
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! ## Compatibility
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! Serialized data can be accessed later as long as:
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! - The underlying schema has not changed
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! - The serialized format has not been changed by format control features
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! - The data was serialized by a semver-compatible version of rkyv
[169](https://docs.rs#169)

An archived SwissTable hash map.

Serializes an `ArchivedBTreeMap` from the given iterator and serializer.

Visits every key-value pair in the B-tree with a function.

If `f` returns `ControlFlow::Break`, `visit` will return `Some` with the
broken value. If `f` returns `Continue` for every pair in the tree,
`visit` will return `None`.

Visits every mutable key-value pair in the B-tree with a function.

If `f` returns `ControlFlow::Break`, `visit` will return `Some` with the
broken value. If `f` returns `Continue` for every pair in the tree,
`visit` will return `None`.

# rkyv::rc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/rc/index.html

## Expand description

Archived versions of shared pointers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# access_unchecked in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/fn.access_unchecked.html

## Expand description

Access a byte slice.

This function does not check that the bytes are valid to access. Use
[ access](https://docs.rs/fn.access.html) to safely access the buffer using validation.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The byte slice must represent a valid archived type when accessed at the
default root position. See the [module docs](https://docs.rs/api/index.html) for more
information.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rkyv::{
    access_unchecked, rancor::Error, to_bytes, Archive, Deserialize,
    Serialize,
};
#[derive(Archive, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Example {
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
let value = Example {
    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,
};
let bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
let archived = unsafe { access_unchecked::<ArchivedExample>(&*bytes) };
assert_eq!(archived.name, "pi");
assert_eq!(archived.value, 31415926);
```

---

# access in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/fn.access.html

Available on

**crate features**only.`alloc` and `bytecheck`## Expand description

Access a byte slice.

This is a safe alternative to [ access_unchecked](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked.html) and is part of the

[high-level API](https://docs.rs/api/high/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rkyv::{
    access, bytecheck::CheckBytes, rancor::Error, to_bytes, Archive,
    Archived, Serialize,
};
#[derive(Archive, Serialize)]
struct Example {
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
let value = Example {
    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,
};
let bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
let archived = access::<ArchivedExample, Error>(&bytes).unwrap();
assert_eq!(archived.name, "pi");
assert_eq!(archived.value, 31415926);
```

---

# rkyv::api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/api/index.html

## Expand description

APIs for producing and using archived data.

[§](https://docs.rs#accessing-byte-slices)Accessing byte slices

The safety requirements for accessing a byte slice will often state that a byte slice must “represent a valid archived type”. The specific validity requirements may vary widely depending on the types being accessed, and so in general the only way to guarantee that this call is safe is to have previously validated the byte slice.

Using techniques such as cryptographic signing can provide a more performant way to verify data integrity from trusted sources.

It is generally safe to assume that unchanged and properly-aligned serialized bytes are always safe to access without validation. By contrast, bytes from a potentially-malicious source should always be validated prior to access.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [high](https://docs.rs/high/index.html)- `alloc`
- APIs for environments where allocations can be made.
- [low](https://docs.rs/low/index.html)
- APIs for environments where allocations cannot be made.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_pos_unchecked.html)- pos_ - unchecked - ⚠
- Access a byte slice with a given root position.
- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_pos_unchecked_mut.html)- pos_ - unchecked_ - mut - ⚠
- Mutably access a byte slice with a given root position.
- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_pos_with_context.html)- pos_ - with_ - context - `bytecheck`
- Access a byte slice with a given root position and context.
- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked.html)- unchecked - ⚠
- Access a byte slice.
- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked_mut.html)- unchecked_ - mut - ⚠
- Mutably access a byte slice.
- [access_](https://docs.rs/fn.access_with_context.html)- with_ - context - `bytecheck`
- Access a byte slice with a given context.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_pos_with_context.html)- pos_ - with_ - context - `bytecheck`
- Check a byte slice with a given root position and context.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_using.html)- using
- Deserialize a value using the given deserializer.
- [root_](https://docs.rs/fn.root_position.html)- position
- Return the position of the root within a buffer of `length`bytes.
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize_using.html)- using
- Serialize a value using the given serializer.

# Archive in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/trait.Archive.html

```
pub trait Archive {
    type
```
[Archived](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Archived): [Portable](https://docs.rs/trait.Portable.html);
    type [Resolver](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Resolver);
    const [COPY_OPTIMIZATION](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.COPY_OPTIMIZATION): [CopyOptimization](https://docs.rs/traits/struct.CopyOptimization.html)<Self> = _;
    // Required method
    fn [resolve](https://docs.rs#tymethod.resolve)(&self, resolver: Self::[Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html#associatedtype.Resolver), out: [Place](https://docs.rs/struct.Place.html)<Self::[Archived](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html#associatedtype.Archived)>);
}## Expand description

A type that can be used without deserializing.

`Archive` is one of three basic traits used to work with zero-copy data and
controls the layout of the data in its archived zero-copy representation.
The [ Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html) trait helps transform types into that representation, and
the

[trait helps transform types back out.](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`Types that implement `Archive` must have a well-defined archived size.
Unsized types can be supported using the [ ArchiveUnsized](https://docs.rs/trait.ArchiveUnsized.html) trait, along
with

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeUnsized.html)

`SerializeUnsized`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.DeserializeUnsized.html)

`DeserializeUnsized`Archiving is done depth-first, writing any data owned by a type before writing the data for the type itself. The type must be able to create the archived type from only its own data and its resolver.

Archived data is always treated as if it is tree-shaped, with the root
owning its direct descendents and so on. Data that is not tree-shaped can be
supported using special serializer and deserializer bounds (see
[ ArchivedRc](https://docs.rs/rc/struct.ArchivedRc.html) for example). In a buffer of
serialized data, objects are laid out in

*reverse order*. This means that the root object is located near the end of the buffer and leaf objects are located near the beginning.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Most of the time, `#[derive(Archive)]` will create an acceptable
implementation. You can use the `#[rkyv(...)]` attribute to control how the
implementation is generated. See the [ Archive](https://docs.rs/derive.Archive.html)
derive macro for more details.

```
use rkyv::{deserialize, rancor::Error, Archive, Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Archive, Deserialize, Serialize, Debug, PartialEq)]
#[rkyv(
    // This will generate a PartialEq impl between our unarchived
    // and archived types
    compare(PartialEq),
    // Derives can be passed through to the generated type:
    derive(Debug),
)]
struct Test {
    int: u8,
    string: String,
    option: Option<Vec<i32>>,
}
fn main() {
    let value = Test {
        int: 42,
        string: "hello world".to_string(),
        option: Some(vec![1, 2, 3, 4]),
    };
    // Serializing is as easy as a single function call
    let _bytes = rkyv::to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
    // Or you can customize your serialization for better performance or control
    // over resource usage
    use rkyv::{api::high::to_bytes_with_alloc, ser::allocator::Arena};
    let mut arena = Arena::new();
    let bytes =
        to_bytes_with_alloc::<_, Error>(&value, arena.acquire()).unwrap();
    // You can use the safe API for fast zero-copy deserialization
    let archived = rkyv::access::<ArchivedTest, Error>(&bytes[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(archived, &value);
    // Or you can use the unsafe API for maximum performance
    let archived =
        unsafe { rkyv::access_unchecked::<ArchivedTest>(&bytes[..]) };
    assert_eq!(archived, &value);
    // And you can always deserialize back to the original type
    let deserialized = deserialize::<Test, Error>(archived).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(deserialized, value);
}
```
*Note: the safe API requires the  bytecheck feature.*

Many of the core and standard library types already have `Archive`
implementations available, but you may need to implement `Archive` for your
own types in some cases the derive macro cannot handle.

In this example, we add our own wrapper that serializes a `&'static str` as
if it’s owned. Normally you can lean on the archived version of `String` to
do most of the work, or use the [ Inline](https://docs.rs/with/struct.Inline.html) to do
exactly this. This example does everything to demonstrate how to implement

`Archive` for your own types.```
use core::{slice, str};
use rkyv::{
    access_unchecked,
    rancor::{Error, Fallible},
    ser::Writer,
    to_bytes,
    Archive, ArchiveUnsized, Archived, Portable, RelPtr, Serialize,
    SerializeUnsized, munge::munge, Place,
};
struct OwnedStr {
    inner: &'static str,
}
#[derive(Portable)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct ArchivedOwnedStr {
    // This will be a relative pointer to our string
    ptr: RelPtr<str>,
}
impl ArchivedOwnedStr {
    // This will help us get the bytes of our type as a str again.
    fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
        unsafe {
            // The as_ptr() function of RelPtr will get a pointer the str
            &*self.ptr.as_ptr()
        }
    }
}
struct OwnedStrResolver {
    // This will be the position that the bytes of our string are stored at.
    // We'll use this to resolve the relative pointer of our
    // ArchivedOwnedStr.
    pos: usize,
}
// The Archive implementation defines the archived version of our type and
// determines how to turn the resolver into the archived form. The Serialize
// implementations determine how to make a resolver from the original value.
impl Archive for OwnedStr {
    type Archived = ArchivedOwnedStr;
    // This is the resolver we can create our Archived version from.
    type Resolver = OwnedStrResolver;
    // The resolve function consumes the resolver and produces the archived
    // value at the given position.
    fn resolve(
        &self,
        resolver: Self::Resolver,
        out: Place<Self::Archived>,
    ) {
        munge!(let ArchivedOwnedStr { ptr } = out);
        RelPtr::emplace_unsized(
            resolver.pos,
            self.inner.archived_metadata(),
            ptr,
        );
    }
}
// We restrict our serializer types with Writer because we need its
// capabilities to serialize the inner string. For other types, we might
// need more or less restrictive bounds on the type of S.
impl<S: Fallible + Writer + ?Sized> Serialize<S> for OwnedStr {
    fn serialize(
        &self,
        serializer: &mut S,
    ) -> Result<Self::Resolver, S::Error> {
        // This is where we want to write the bytes of our string and return
        // a resolver that knows where those bytes were written.
        // We also need to serialize the metadata for our str.
        Ok(OwnedStrResolver {
            pos: self.inner.serialize_unsized(serializer)?,
        })
    }
}
const STR_VAL: &'static str = "I'm in an OwnedStr!";
let value = OwnedStr { inner: STR_VAL };
// It works!
let buf = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).expect("failed to serialize");
let archived =
    unsafe { access_unchecked::<ArchivedOwnedStr>(buf.as_ref()) };
// Let's make sure our data got written correctly
assert_eq!(archived.as_str(), STR_VAL);
```
## Provided Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#provided-associated-consts)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rkyv/traits.rs.html#227-228)#### const [COPY_OPTIMIZATION](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.COPY_OPTIMIZATION): [CopyOptimization](https://docs.rs/traits/struct.CopyOptimization.html)<Self> = _

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rkyv/traits.rs.html#227-228)

#### const [COPY_OPTIMIZATION](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.COPY_OPTIMIZATION): [CopyOptimization](https://docs.rs/traits/struct.CopyOptimization.html)<Self> = _

An optimization flag that allows the bytes of this type to be copied
directly to a writer instead of calling `serialize`.

This optimization is disabled by default. To enable this optimization,
you must unsafely attest that `Self` is trivially copyable using
[ CopyOptimization::enable](https://docs.rs/traits/struct.CopyOptimization.html#method.enable) or

[.](https://docs.rs/traits/struct.CopyOptimization.html#method.enable_if)

`CopyOptimization::enable_if`## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Creates the archived version of this value at the given position and writes it to the given output.

The output should be initialized field-by-field rather than by writing a whole struct. Performing a typed copy will mark all of the padding bytes as uninitialized, but they must remain set to the value they currently have. This prevents leaking uninitialized memory to the final archive.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# ArchiveUnsized in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/trait.ArchiveUnsized.html

`pub trait ArchiveUnsized: `[Pointee](https://docs.rs/ptr_meta/0.3.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ptr_meta/trait.Pointee.html) {
    type [Archived](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Archived): [ArchivePointee](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ArchivePointee.html) + [Portable](https://docs.rs/trait.Portable.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html);
    // Required method
    fn [archived_metadata](https://docs.rs#tymethod.archived_metadata)(&self) -> [ArchivedMetadata](https://docs.rs/type.ArchivedMetadata.html)<Self>;
}## Expand description

A counterpart of [ Archive](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html) that’s suitable for unsized types.

Unlike `Archive`, types that implement `ArchiveUnsized` must be serialized
separately from their owning object. For example, whereas an `i32` might be
laid out as part of a larger struct, a `Box<i32>` would serialize the `i32`
somewhere in the archive and the `Box` would point to it as part of the
larger struct. Because of this, the equivalent
[ Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html#associatedtype.Resolver) type for

`ArchiveUnsized` is always a
`usize` representing the position of the serialized value.`ArchiveUnsized` is automatically implemented for all types that implement
[ Archive](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html). Nothing special needs to be done to use them with types like

`Box`, `Rc`, and `Arc`. It is also already implemented for slices and string
slices, and the `rkyv_dyn` crate can be used to archive trait objects. Other
unsized types must manually implement `ArchiveUnsized`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This example shows how to manually implement `ArchiveUnsized` for an unsized
type. Special care must be taken to ensure that the types are laid out
correctly.

```
use core::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};
use ptr_meta::Pointee;
use rkyv::{
    access_unchecked,
    primitive::ArchivedUsize,
    rancor::{Error, Fallible},
    ser::{Positional, Writer, WriterExt as _},
    to_bytes,
    traits::ArchivePointee,
    Archive, ArchiveUnsized, Archived, ArchivedMetadata, Portable, RelPtr,
    Serialize, SerializeUnsized,
};
// We're going to be dealing mostly with blocks that have a trailing slice
#[derive(Portable)]
#[repr(C)]
pub struct Block<H, T: ?Sized> {
    head: H,
    tail: T,
}
unsafe impl<H, T> Pointee for Block<H, [T]> {
    type Metadata = <[T] as Pointee>::Metadata;
}
// ArchivePointee is automatically derived for sized types because pointers
// to sized types don't need to store any extra information. Because we're
// making an unsized block, we need to define what metadata gets stored with
// our data pointer.
impl<H, T> ArchivePointee for Block<H, [T]> {
    // This is the extra data that needs to get stored for blocks with
    // trailing slices
    type ArchivedMetadata = <[T] as ArchivePointee>::ArchivedMetadata;
    // We need to be able to turn our archived metadata into regular
    // metadata for our type
    fn pointer_metadata(
        metadata: &Self::ArchivedMetadata,
    ) -> <Self as Pointee>::Metadata {
        metadata.to_native() as usize
    }
}
// We're implementing ArchiveUnsized for just Block<H, [T]>. We can still
// implement Archive for blocks with sized tails and they won't conflict.
impl<H: Archive, T: Archive> ArchiveUnsized for Block<H, [T]> {
    // We'll reuse our block type as our archived type.
    type Archived = Block<Archived<H>, [Archived<T>]>;
    // Here's where we make the metadata for our archived type.
    fn archived_metadata(&self) -> ArchivedMetadata<Self> {
        // Because the metadata for our `ArchivedBlock` is the metadata of
        // the trailing slice, we just need to return that archived
        // metadata.
        self.tail.archived_metadata()
    }
}
// The bounds we use on our serializer type indicate that we need basic
// serializer capabilities, and then whatever capabilities our head and tail
// types need to serialize themselves.
impl<H, T, S> SerializeUnsized<S> for Block<H, [T]>
where
    H: Serialize<S>,
    T: Serialize<S>,
    S: Fallible + Writer + ?Sized,
{
    // This is where we construct our unsized type in the serializer
    fn serialize_unsized(
        &self,
        serializer: &mut S,
    ) -> Result<usize, S::Error> {
        // First, we serialize the head and all the tails. This will make
        // sure that when we finally build our block, we don't accidentally
        // mess up the structure with serialized dependencies.
        let head_resolver = self.head.serialize(serializer)?;
        let mut resolvers = Vec::new();
        for tail in self.tail.iter() {
            resolvers.push(tail.serialize(serializer)?);
        }
        // Now we align our serializer for our archived type and resolve it.
        // We can't align for unsized types so we treat the trailing slice
        // like an array of 0 length for now.
        let result = serializer
            .align_for::<Block<Archived<H>, [Archived<T>; 0]>>()?;
        unsafe {
            serializer.resolve_aligned(&self.head, head_resolver)?;
        }
        serializer.align_for::<Archived<T>>()?;
        for (item, resolver) in self.tail.iter().zip(resolvers.drain(..)) {
            unsafe {
                serializer.resolve_aligned(item, resolver)?;
            }
        }
        Ok(result)
    }
}
let value = Box::new(Block {
    head: "Numbers 1-4".to_string(),
    tail: [1, 2, 3, 4],
});
// We have a Box<Block<String, [i32; 4]>> but we want to it to be a
// Box<Block<String, [i32]>>, so we need manually "unsize" the pointer.
let ptr = Box::into_raw(value);
let unsized_ptr = ptr_meta::from_raw_parts_mut::<Block<String, [i32]>>(
    ptr.cast::<()>(),
    4,
);
let unsized_value = unsafe { Box::from_raw(unsized_ptr) };
let bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&unsized_value).unwrap();
let archived = unsafe {
    access_unchecked::<Archived<Box<Block<String, [i32]>>>>(&bytes)
};
assert_eq!(archived.head, "Numbers 1-4");
assert_eq!(archived.tail.len(), 4);
assert_eq!(archived.tail, [1, 2, 3, 4]);
```

# Deserialize in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<T, D: `[Fallible](https://docs.rs/rancor/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rancor/trait.Fallible.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)> {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)(&self, deserializer: [&mut D](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/rancor/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rancor/trait.Fallible.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Converts a type back from its archived form.

Some types may require specific deserializer capabilities, such as `Rc` and
`Arc`. In these cases, the deserializer type `D` should be bound so that it
implements traits that provide those capabilities (e.g.
[ Pooling](https://docs.rs/de/trait.Pooling.html)).

This can be derived with [ Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Portable in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/trait.Portable.html

`pub unsafe trait Portable { }`## Expand description

A type with a stable, well-defined layout that is the same on all targets.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The implementing type must have a stable, well-defined layout that is the
same on all targets. Structs and unions must be `#[repr(transparent)]` or
`#[repr(C)]`. Enums must be `#[repr(C)]`, `#[repr(int)]`, or `#[repr(C, int)]`.

The implementing type must not have interior mutability (i.e. no
`UnsafeCell`s).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Serialize in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/trait.Serialize.html

`pub trait Serialize<S: `[Fallible](https://docs.rs/rancor/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rancor/trait.Fallible.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>: [Archive](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)(&self, serializer: [&mut S](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html#associatedtype.Resolver), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/rancor/0.1.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rancor/trait.Fallible.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Converts a type to its archived form.

Objects perform any supportive serialization during
[ serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html#tymethod.serialize). For types that reference nonlocal
(pointed-to) data, this is when that data must be serialized to the output.
These types will need to bound

`S` to implement
[and any other required traits (e.g.](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.Writer.html)

`Writer`[). They should then serialize their dependencies during](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.Sharing.html)

`Sharing``serialize`.See [ Archive](https://docs.rs/trait.Archive.html) for examples of implementing

`Serialize`.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# access_mut in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/fn.access_mut.html

Available on

**crate features**only.`alloc` and `bytecheck`## Expand description

Mutably access a byte slice.

This is a safe alternative to [ access_unchecked_mut](https://docs.rs/fn.access_unchecked_mut.html) and is part of the

[high-level API](https://docs.rs/api/high/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rkyv::{
    access_mut,
    bytecheck::CheckBytes,
    rancor::Error, munge::munge,
    to_bytes, Archive, Archived, Serialize,
};
#[derive(Archive, Serialize)]
struct Example {
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
let value = Example {
    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,
};
let mut bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
let mut archived = access_mut::<ArchivedExample, Error>(&mut bytes)
    .unwrap();
// Because the access is mutable, we can mutate the archived data
munge!(let ArchivedExample { mut value, .. } = archived);
assert_eq!(*value, 31415926);
*value = 12345.into();
assert_eq!(*value, 12345);
```

---

# access_unchecked_mut in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/fn.access_unchecked_mut.html

## Expand description

Mutably access a byte slice.

This function does not check that the bytes are valid to access. Use
[ access_mut](https://docs.rs/fn.access_mut.html) to safely access the buffer using
validation.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The byte slice must represent a valid archived type when accessed at the
default root position. See the [module docs](https://docs.rs/api/index.html) for more
information.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rkyv::{
    to_bytes, access_unchecked_mut, util::Align, Archive,
    munge::munge, Serialize, Deserialize, rancor::Error,
};
#[derive(Archive, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Example {
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
let value = Example {
    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,
};
let mut bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
let mut archived = unsafe {
    access_unchecked_mut::<ArchivedExample>(&mut *bytes)
};
assert_eq!(archived.name, "pi");
assert_eq!(archived.value, 31415926);
// Because the access is mutable, we can mutate the archived data
munge!(let ArchivedExample { mut value, .. } = archived);
assert_eq!(*value, 31415926);
*value = 12345.into();
assert_eq!(*value, 12345);
```

---

# deserialize in rkyv - Rust

pub fn deserialize<T, E>(
    value: &impl
```
[Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)<T, [HighDeserializer](https://docs.rs/api/high/type.HighDeserializer.html)<E>>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<T, E>Available on

**crate feature**only.`alloc`## Expand description

Deserialize a value from the given archived value.

This is part of the [high-level API](https://docs.rs/api/high/index.html).

```
use rkyv::{
    access, deserialize, rancor::Error, to_bytes, Archive, Deserialize,
    Serialize,
};

    name: String,
    value: i32,

let value = Example {
    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,
};
let bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
let archived = access::<ArchivedExample, Error>(&*bytes).unwrap();
let deserialized = deserialize::<Example, Error>(archived).unwrap();
assert_eq!(deserialized, value);

**crate features**only.`alloc` and `bytecheck`## Expand description

    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,

# from_bytes_unchecked in rkyv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rkyv/0.8.17/rkyv/fn.from_bytes_unchecked.html

**crate feature**only.

`alloc`## Expand description

Deserialize a value from the given bytes.

This function does not check that the data is valid. Use [ from_bytes](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes.html) to
validate the data instead.

This is part of the [high-level API](https://docs.rs/api/high/index.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The byte slice must represent a valid archived type when accessed at the
default root position. See the [module docs](https://docs.rs/api/index.html) for more
information.

```
use rkyv::{
    from_bytes_unchecked, rancor::Error, to_bytes, Archive, Deserialize,
    Serialize,
};
#[derive(Archive, Serialize, Deserialize, Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Example {
    name: String,
    value: i32,
}
let value = Example {
    name: "pi".to_string(),
    value: 31415926,
};
let bytes = to_bytes::<Error>(&value).unwrap();
let deserialized =
    unsafe { from_bytes_unchecked::<Example, Error>(&bytes).unwrap() };
assert_eq!(deserialized, value);
```
